newsitem.title: USA: Dow jumps 153 points; bonds, dollar rise.
newsitem.headline: Dow jumps 153 points; bonds, dollar rise.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks staged a powerful rebound on Tuesday, lifting bonds and the dollar, as the market shrugged off remarks by the Japanese prime minister that triggered Monday's massive sell-off.
Cocoa prices stormed to a nine-year high amid speculative buying sparked partly by growing concern about the impact on crops of a potential change in global weather patterns.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 153.80 points, or 2.02 percent, at 7,758.06 after Monday's 192-point drop, which was the second-steepest fall ever for the blue-chip index. The Dow is now back within near distance of last Friday's record close of 7,796.51.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 18.11 points, or 1.26 percent, to its 17th record high of the year at 1,452.43, propelled by gains in technology stocks.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,787 to 962 on active volume of 542 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Stocks rallied quickly as Japan moved overnight to calm Wall Street's fears that Japan might sell some of its huge U.S. Treasury holdings.

On Monday, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech in New York, said that Japan had been tempted in the past to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.
Japan came to the market's rescue overnight and reassured financial markets that the country was not planning an imminent sale of its U.S. government bond holdings.
"The (Japanese prime minister's) comments seemed off-the-cuff. When people really took a look at them, they decided to get back in," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage.
The market's comeback surprised many traders, particularly the strength of a late-day rally which drove the Dow, already up 50 points, climbing more than 100 points in the last 90 minutes of trading.
"The market seems to be able to weather any bad news. It shakes it off and goes back on its merry way," said Ducey.
The 30-year Treasury rose 5/32, or $1.5625 on a $1,000 bond, reducing its yield to 6.69 percent from 6.70 percent at Monday's close. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
The dollar rose to 114.83 Japanese yen from 114.74 late Monday and to 1.7232 German marks from 1.7175.

At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, cocoa for July delivery rose to a peak of $1,700 a metric ton, the highest level for a nearby contract since May 1988. July closed $17 up on the day at $1,680.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, copper prices sank to a six-week low as the U.S. physical market succumbed to a seasonal summer slowdown.
Copper for July delivery fell to a low of 111.60 cents a pound before closing 6.05 cents weaker at 112.15 cents.

Crude oil also closed lower on the New York Mercantile Exchange as early-session strength evaporated after Iraq's oil minister said he expected his country to resume oil exports in the next week to 10 days.
August crude settled 11 cents off at $19.03 a barrel. July gasoline ended 0.04 cent up at 55.68 cents a gallon, while July heating oil finished off 0.35 cent at 51.57 cents a gallon.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,596.3, up 20.5 points, or 0.45 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,341.93, down 94.21 points, or 0.46 percent.
